one_line: Mike Spitz (PFF) reports a Jan–Mar 2026 case study where agent-driven spec, design doc, ticket and PR flow cut delivery time and dropped Scrum for a 20-engineer team.
summary: Mike Spitz, speaking for PFF (a sports data company with a consumer fantasy and betting arm), describes a case study run from January to March where two strong engineers used an agent-driven workflow. The flow goes from a spec, to an agent interview, to a lightweight design doc (LDD) generated by a skill, to auto-created tickets and PRs. He reports about 25x more deploys and roughly 10x blended output versus a 10-person team, with a feature that was estimated at four months finishing in under two. He caveats that small teams are naturally faster, and says output only matters if customers are happier, citing a survey score of 8.6/10 versus about 7 to 7.5 before. Sprint planning, standups, refinement and project managers were dropped and replaced by huddles, auto-updated tickets and customer-survey retros. He stresses a slow, phased rollout that starts with the best engineers on non-critical systems, verifiable deterministic checks, agent code review for style nits, and composable per-step skills. Humans remain needed for security, product feel and scope control.

key_ideas.idea: Measure output by customer happiness, not PRs or code volume
key_ideas.detail: PFF blended ticket count with code complexity to get a 10x output figure, but the speaker says the real test is customer satisfaction. Surveys rose to 8.6/10 from about 7 to 7.5 before AI.

key_ideas.idea: Remove the ceremonies that existed because engineers were the bottleneck
key_ideas.detail: With engineering no longer the constraint, sprint planning, estimation, standups, refinement and the project manager role were dropped. Huddles every other day with engineers, product and design replaced them.

key_ideas.idea: Spec and design doc are the real planning layer
key_ideas.detail: An agent interviews the author about the spec, then a skill writes an LDD that matches past LDDs. The LDD is circulated for engineer feedback, and tickets and PRs are generated from it.

key_ideas.idea: Let PR state drive ticket state and make tickets non-blocking
key_ideas.detail: Ticket status follows the PR: open becomes in progress, review updates it, merge closes it. Generated tickets are structured to avoid blocking each other, and any real dependencies are flagged.

key_ideas.idea: Offload nit-level code review to agents, keep humans on the big picture
key_ideas.detail: Agents handle style and opinion-based comments that engineers dislike giving or receiving, which removes the emotional friction. Humans still review design and architecture.

key_ideas.idea: Verifiable deterministic checks come before autonomy
key_ideas.detail: Tests, feature flags for trunk-based development, and product-specific generated analytics give agents checkable targets. Guardrails should work before autonomous flows run.

key_ideas.idea: Treat the lifecycle as a factory and turn each step into a composable skill
key_ideas.detail: Break the flow into small parts such as branch naming, feature flags and an API pattern, then encode each as a skill. Be wary of third-party skills whose opinions conflict with your own engineering standards.

key_ideas.idea: Post-merge QA agent checks acceptance criteria; self-healing is planned
key_ideas.detail: Each merge deploys to staging, then a QA agent checks the tickets against acceptance criteria and reports failures. The speaker plans to have an agent turn those failures into fix PRs, but says this is not built yet.

key_ideas.idea: Start with the best engineers, boring tasks and a slow phased rollout
key_ideas.detail: Begin with the strongest engineers on tasks people dislike, in non-critical systems first. Giving everyone a coding agent and a hackathon did not work for others, because every org's style is different.

techniques.name: Agent-interviewed spec then skill-generated LDD
techniques.how: An agent interviews the author to sharpen the spec. A skill then drafts a lightweight design doc by analysing past LDDs so new work matches existing patterns. Circulate it for feedback before generating tickets.
techniques.when: Use before any agent builds a feature, to stop over-engineering and keep style consistent across a codebase.

techniques.name: Auto-generated, non-blocking tickets and PR-driven status
techniques.how: Generate tickets from the approved LDD and structure them so none block each other, flagging real dependencies. Sync ticket status from PR events (open, review, merge).
techniques.when: Use when a team wants to drop standups and sprint refinement while keeping an accurate board.

techniques.name: Agent code review limited to opinion-level nits
techniques.how: Run an agent over PRs for style, naming and convention issues, and leave architecture and design to human reviewers.
techniques.when: Use when human reviewers spend time on style comments and you want their attention on design.

techniques.name: Post-staging QA agent against acceptance criteria
techniques.how: On merge, deploy to staging, then spawn a QA agent that reads the ticket acceptance criteria and tests each one. It reports failures per item. Planned extension: an agent turns failures into fix PRs.
techniques.when: Use to verify agent-written features automatically before human QA.

techniques.name: Composable per-step skills for the delivery lifecycle
techniques.how: Write one skill per lifecycle step (branch naming, feature flags, API design pattern) and compose them. Review third-party skills for conflicting opinions before adopting them.
techniques.when: Use when you want consistent output across many agents and repos.

techniques.name: Customer survey as the primary retro signal
techniques.how: Run statistically significant customer surveys each cycle and track deploy frequency. Ask engineers to flag problems immediately, not at sprint end.
techniques.when: Use when you need a retro metric that reflects product value rather than activity.

techniques.name: Phased, non-critical-first rollout
techniques.how: Pick the most capable engineers, run proof-of-concept features in low-stakes systems, then move to high-traffic products once guardrails hold.
techniques.when: Use when adopting agents in an existing org with mixed engineering styles.

numbers.claim: PFF has about 100M page views per year and about 9M fantasy drafts per year, with roughly 200 employees and about 20 engineers.

Two engineers deployed about 5 times a day, versus about one deploy every 5 days for a team of around 10. The speaker calls this 25x more deploys, with a caveat that a smaller team is naturally faster.
Blended ticket and code-complexity output for the two-engineer team was about 10x the baseline.
A feature set was built in under 2 months, against an estimate of about 4 months the old way.
One engineer was unblocked in under a month, versus both engineers blocked for about 3 months under the old process.
Average customer quality score was 8.6/10 after the change, versus about 7 to 7.5 before AI.
The case study ran from January to March (about 2-3 months).

hot_takes: Scrum did not survive the change, and sprint planning and estimation add no value once engineering is no longer the bottleneck.
Small companies have a structural advantage over large enterprises in rolling this out.
Engineers who are curious will thrive, while those who need prescriptive specs will struggle.
Teams will likely need to estimate token spend per feature once vendor token subsidies end.
Giving everyone a coding agent and a hackathon is why many AI rollouts have stalled.

relevance.why: ProsHarness plans, critiques and checkpoints agent runs. The talk's spec-interview, generated LDD and post-merge QA-against-acceptance-criteria loop is a close pattern for its plan and verify stages.
relevance.action: Add a stage to ProsHarness plan mode where an agent interviews the user on the spec and writes a design doc from prior docs. Then add a verifier that checks acceptance criteria after each run and reports per-item failures.

relevance.why: The talk covers delivery process for product teams. It does not touch AgentOS infra such as proxying, memory, inference or sandboxing.
Useful as a case-study reference for how a small team sequences agent adoption, phasing and guardrails.
relevance.action: Read the talk's rollout guidance (start with the best engineers and non-critical systems) before proposing agent workflows to a team.
